bib.title: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering", Chan Jun Shern, Chowdhury, Jaffe, Aung, Sherburn, Mays, Starace, Liu, Maksin, Patwardhan, Weng, Mądry (OpenAI). Venue as printed: "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025". arXiv:2410.07095v6, 26 Feb 2025.

COVERAGE: 29 of 29 pages, 89,194 of 89,194 chars, including appendices A.1-A.9. References (pp. 11-13) and Table 8's per-competition split list (pp. 19-24) were skimmed. The Figure 3 and 4 curves are images, so only the points quoted in text were read.

CLAIMS

- claim: The headline score is the share of attempts that earn any Kaggle medal, judged against each competition's Private leaderboard snapshot.
  number: bronze = top 40% (under 250 teams), top 100 (250-999 teams), top 10% (1000+ teams)
  setup: 75 competitions; medal logic applied to all, including ones that never awarded medals; leaderboard snapshots taken May-August 2024
  quote: "we calculate the percentage of attempts that are awarded any medal (bronze and above)"; "Only nine humans have ever achieved medals on 75 different Kaggle competitions"
  where: p4, Section 2.2 and Table 1

- claim: The best setup medals in about one competition in six.
  number: 16.9 ± 1.1% for o1-preview; 8.7 ± 0.5% for GPT-4o
  setup: AIDE scaffold, 24 h per competition, one A10 GPU, 16 seeds (o1-preview) and 36 seeds (GPT-4o), mean ± one standard error
  quote: "o1-preview 98.4 ± 0.4 82.8 ± 1.1 29.4 ± 1.3 3.4 ± 0.5 4.1 ± 0.6 9.4 ± 0.8 16.9 ± 1.1"
  where: p6, Table 2

- claim: More attempts roughly double the score.
  number: 16.9% at pass@1 to 34.1% at pass@8 (o1-preview); GPT-4o pass@6 = 17.0%
  setup: AIDE; pass@k estimated from n seeds for k up to n/2
  quote: "o1-preview's score doubles from 16.9% using pass@1 to 34.1% using pass@8"; "GPT-4o (AIDE) with pass@6 achieves a comparable score ( 17.0%) to o1-preview (AIDE) with pass@1 (16.9%)"
  where: p2; p7, Figure 3

- claim: More time helps modestly.
  number: 8.7% at 24 h to 11.8% at 100 h
  setup: GPT-4o with AIDE, node cap raised 10x to 5,000, hourly snapshots; seed count not stated
  quote: "GPT-4o scores 8.7% given 24 hours to attempt each competition, but 11.8% when given 100 hours"
  where: p2; pp. 7-8, Section 3.4 and Figure 4. Most medals come in the first couple of hours, and the count sometimes falls because AIDE picks its "best" attempt imperfectly.

- claim: Changing hardware made no clear difference.
  number: CPU-only 9.1 ± 1.0; Standard 8.7 ± 0.5; two GPUs 10.2 ± 2.0
  setup: GPT-4o with AIDE, 3 seeds (Standard 36)
  quote: "Surprisingly, we find that GPT-4o (AIDE) performs similarly in all experiments."
  where: p7, Table 3. The agent never tried to use the second GPU in the logs inspected.

- claim: The scaffold matters as much as the model.
  number: 8.7% (AIDE) vs 0.8% (MLAB) vs 4.4% (OpenHands)
  setup: GPT-4o, 3 seeds for MLAB and OpenHands
  quote: "(8.7% vs. 0.8% and 4.4% respectively), despite making a similar number of valid submissions"
  where: p5

- claim: Seeds and error bars are reported throughout.
  number: 3 seeds by default
  setup: all experiments unless stated
  quote: "We repeat all experiments with 3 seeds (that is, 3 runs per competition) to compute the mean and standard error unless otherwise specified."
  where: p5

- claim: Obfuscating the competition descriptions did not lower the score.
  number: Original 8.5 ± 0.6; Obfuscated 8.4 ± 1.0
  setup: GPT-4o with AIDE, 10 seeds, all 75 descriptions manually rewritten
  quote: "Original 8.5 ± 0.6 Obfuscated 8.4 ± 1.0"
  where: p9, Table 4

- claim: Familiarity with a competition does not predict performance on it.
  number: Pearson -0.24, p = 0.04
  setup: GPT-4o base model; familiarity = mean token probability on the competition page plus the 5 most popular discussion posts
  quote: "Pearson's correlation: -0.24, p-value: 0.04"
  where: p8, Figure 5

- claim: No plagiarism or rule-breaking was found.
  number: 60% Dolos similarity threshold against the top 50 notebooks
  setup: run on medal-winning submissions only; log flags were reviewed by humans and all judged false positives
  quote: "We surface any submission file with a similarity score above 60% for human review of potential plagiarism, finding no detected cases of plagiarism."
  where: p15, A.4; Table 6 (the o1-preview "manually-written submission" flag rate was 14.1%, all false positives)

- claim: The benchmark is expensive to run.
  number: 1800 GPU hours per seed; 127.5M input and 15.0M output tokens
  setup: 24 h x 75 competitions; token figures are o1-preview with AIDE, one seed
  quote: "o1-preview with AIDE used 127.5M input tokens and 15.0M output tokens on average for one seed of 75 competitions"
  where: p10

- claim: Difficulty tiers separate the scores sharply.
  number: Low 34.3 ± 2.4; Medium 8.8 ± 1.1; High 10.0 ± 1.9
  setup: o1-preview with AIDE
  quote: "o1-preview 34.3 ± 2.4 8.8 ± 1.1 10.0 ± 1.9 16.9 ± 1.1"
  where: p28, Table 9. Figure 9 shows medals on 2013-2022 competitions and few after 2022.

LIMITS

Conceded by the authors:
- Models may have trained on all public Kaggle material, including the test sets. Footnote 13 says GPT-4's base model reproduced rows of the Titanic dataset.
- Reuse of high-level strategies is hard to detect. The contamination result "make[s] no guarantees about future models".
- The train/test splits and the grading code are re-implemented, so scores are only approximately comparable to the human leaderboard.
- Agents have newer tools than the original competitors.
- The tasks are clean and well specified, unlike real R&D.

Not shown:
- Contamination was tested on GPT-4o only, not on o1-preview, which is the headline model.
- Plagiarism and rule checks cover medal-winning runs only.
- pass@k counts a medal on any of k attempts as graded on the test set. The agent has no way to make that selection itself, and the paper does not discuss this.
- No dollar cost is given.
- Grading is outcome-only (a CSV). Trajectories are inspected only for rule-breaking.
- The paper does not say how the standard error is pooled across seeds and competitions.
- Humans had weeks or months; agents had 24 h.
- The paper reads the familiarity result as "no correlation", but the printed statistic is a negative correlation at p = 0.04.
- The model set is dated (o1-preview, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1).

BUILDS ON: pass@k from Chen et al. (2021); AIDE (Schmidt et al., 2024); MLAgentBench (Huang et al., 2024b); OpenHands (Wang et al., 2024); Dolos (Maertens et al., 2024); the familiarity measure from Carlini et al. (2023); the contamination definition from Dekoninck et al. (2024); medal thresholds from Kaggle (2024).

CODE: none worth keeping. The pass@k formula on p7 is garbled in extraction; it is the standard 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k), averaged over competitions.

FIGURES: Figure 3, p7: "The percentage of medals achieved increases with the number of attempts allowed." One plot shows that attempt count moves the score as much as swapping the model does (GPT-4o at pass@6 is about o1-preview at pass@1).

PROBLEMS

- Extraction is clean apart from the pass@k formula.
- Figure 8 (p17) reproduces the agent prompt, which contains imperative instructions ("you MUST produce a submission file..."). I treated it as data and ignored it.
- Internal inconsistencies in the paper:
  - The rule-breaking tool is GPT-4o on p5 and GPT-4o mini on p15.
  - The AIDE cap is "500 nodes" on p6, while Table 7 has agent.steps 2000.
  - Low complexity is 30% on p3 and 29% in Figure 6.
  - Figure 6 says 15 categories; Table 10 lists 19.
  - Table 2 and Table 9 totals differ: GPT-4o AIDE 8.7 vs 8.6, MLAB 0.8 vs 1.3, OpenHands 4.4 vs 5.1.
  - The "Original" baseline in Table 4 is 8.5, against 8.7 elsewhere.
  - The doubling is stated at pass@8 on p2 and at pass@6 in the Figure 3 caption.
